questions.q: "Orders placed before 2 pm ship today, unless it is a public holiday." Which condition says when an order ships today?
questions.explain: "A unless B" means "A if not B", which is a && !b. The OR version would ship every order on a normal day, even one placed at 9 pm.

questions.q: "Neither suspended nor banned users may post." Which expression is true for a user who may post?
questions.explain: "Neither A nor B" is "not A and not B", which is also !(a || b). The OR version and !(a && b) would let a suspended-but-not-banned user post.

questions.q: "Free delivery on orders over ₦20,000, but only in Lagos." Logically, what does "but" mean here?
questions.explain: "But" signals a contrast in English, yet logically both parts must hold: a big order and a Lagos address.

questions.q: "A customer may withdraw only if the account is active." Which statement follows from this rule alone?
questions.explain: "Only if" states a necessary condition: without it, no withdrawal. It does not say being active is sufficient; other conditions can still apply.
options: An inactive account may never withdraw
Being active is enough to withdraw
Locked accounts may withdraw if active

questions.q: In the rule isAdmin || isOwner, what is isAdmin?
questions.explain: In an OR-rule, each part alone guarantees the result (sufficient), but none is required, because the other part can also satisfy it (not necessary).

questions.q: A rule says "customers over 18". Which operator is the literal meaning, and what should you do if you suspect the author meant 18 to count?
questions.explain: "Over" excludes the boundary. Boundary words are often used loosely, so asking is cheap; fixing a wrong boundary in production is not.
options: age > 18, and ask the business whether 18 itself is allowed

questions.q: By De Morgan's laws, what is !(bigOrder && inLagos)?
questions.explain: Negate each part and swap AND with OR. Failing either requirement is enough to lose free delivery.

questions.q: By De Morgan's laws, what is !(isAdmin || isOwner)?
questions.explain: To be refused by an OR-rule, you must fail every way in: not admin and not owner.

questions.q: What is the opposite of active && !locked && hasFunds?
questions.explain: Negate each part (!locked becomes locked) and turn every AND into OR. The opposite of a checklist is "at least one box is unticked".

questions.q: What is the exact opposite of balance >= amount?
questions.explain: When balance equals amount, the original is true, so the opposite must be false there. Only < does that.

questions.q: Nights must be from 1 to 30: nights >= 1 && nights <= 30. Which guard refuses exactly the invalid values?
questions.explain: De Morgan swaps AND for OR, and each comparison flips with its boundary: >= becomes <, <= becomes >. The AND version can never be true, since no number is below 1 and above 30.

questions.q: What is wrong with status !== "shipped" || status !== "delivered"?
questions.explain: "Neither shipped nor delivered" is !(shipped || delivered), which De Morgan turns into two !== checks joined with AND.
options: Nothing; it means "neither shipped nor delivered"
It is always true, because every status differs from at least one of the two
It throws an error for unknown statuses

questions.q: Why does if (role === "admin" || "manager") let every user in?
questions.explain: Each side of || must be a complete condition: role === "admin" || role === "manager".
options: Because it is read as (role === "admin") || "manager", and "manager" is a truthy string

questions.q: What does !account.locked && account.active mean?
questions.explain: ! binds tightest, so it applies only to account.locked. To negate a group, wrap the group in parentheses.

questions.q: What is the simplest equivalent of age >= 18 && age >= 21?
questions.explain: Anyone aged 21 or more is also 18 or more, so the stricter part implies the other and the looser part adds nothing to the AND.

questions.q: What is the simplest equivalent of isAdmin || (isAdmin && isOwner)?
questions.explain: Absorption: whenever the group isAdmin && isOwner is true, isAdmin is already true, so the group never changes the answer.

questions.q: Which is equivalent to (isMember && hasCoupon) || (isMember && isSale)?
questions.explain: Factor out the shared part, like 2×3 + 2×5 = 2×(3+5). Without the parentheses, a non-member during a sale would get the discount.

questions.q: How can if (balance >= amount) { return true; } else { return false; } be simplified?
questions.explain: The condition already is the boolean you want to return. (!(balance <= amount) is balance > amount, which is wrong at the boundary.)

questions.q: You simplified a condition with three boolean inputs. How can you be sure the new one behaves the same?
questions.explain: Three booleans have only 23 = 8 combinations. If old and new agree on all of them, they are equivalent: that is a proof, not a guess.
options: Try two or three typical inputs
Compare old and new on all 8 combinations with nested loops
Check that the new one is shorter

questions.q: You cannot loop over every possible age. Which test values best check age >= 21 against another version of the rule?
questions.explain: Comparisons can only disagree near their boundaries. Test just below, exactly on and just above each boundary, plus far values on both sides.

questions.q: How do guard clauses relate to De Morgan's laws?
questions.explain: !(a && b && c) is !a || !b || !c. Each guard is one of those negated parts, with its own message; the function says yes only after all of them are false.
options: They do not; guards are only about style
The opposite of an AND-rule is an OR of negated parts, and each guard checks one of those parts
Guards turn every OR into AND
Guards remove the need to negate anything

questions.q: A locked account also has too little money. Why check locked before balance?
questions.explain: The final allowed/refused answer does not depend on guard order, but the reason does. Security and state checks go first; details about the request come after.
options: Because it changes whether the withdrawal is allowed
Because the reason shown should not leak balance details to someone who may not own the account
Because JavaScript requires boolean checks before number checks

questions.q: Why does checkWithdrawal start with a guard for a non-whole or non-positive amount, although the business rule never mentioned it?
questions.explain: Business rules describe normal requests. Your code must also handle abnormal inputs, and in money code they are exactly what an attacker would try.
options: Because a negative "withdrawal" would add money, and inputs the rule forgot must still be refused
Because numbers must always be checked last

questions.q: What does "fail closed" mean for a guard-clause function?
questions.explain: The "yes" is the last line. Each guard can only refuse. Adding a guard can only make the function stricter, never accidentally more permissive.
options: It closes the program on error
It returns "allowed" only after every check passed, so a missing piece of information leads to a refusal
It starts from "allowed" and looks for reasons to refuse

questions.explain: "Does not exceed" allows exactly ₦100,000. The guard is the negation of <=, which is >, so only 40001 is refused.

questions.q: Fix canCancel so an order can be cancelled only when its status is neither "shipped" nor "delivered".
questions.explain: "Neither A nor B" is "not A and not B". With || the condition is always true.

questions.q: Write refused(active, locked, hasFunds) as the exact opposite of active && !locked && hasFunds, using De Morgan and no outer !( … ). The loop checks it on all 8 rows.
questions.explain: Negate each part (!locked becomes locked) and swap every && for ||. The loop checks that refused equals !allowed on every row.

questions.q: Fix canSeeReports so that only admins and managers get true.
questions.explain: Each side of || must be a full comparison. "manager" on its own is a truthy string, so the original returned it for every non-admin.

questions.q: Write checkBooking(guest, nights) with guard clauses: return "please log in" when there is no guest, "nights must be 1 to 30" when nights is not a whole number from 1 to 30, and "booked" otherwise.
questions.explain: The opposite of nights >= 1 && nights <= 30 is nights < 1 || nights > 30. The boundaries 1 and 30 are allowed.

please log in
nights must be 1 to 30
booked
booked

questions.q: Write newDiscount as a simpler version of oldDiscount (factor out the shared part). The checker compares them on all 8 rows.
questions.explain: Both groups need isMember, so it can be factored out, like 2×3 + 2×5 = 2×(3+5). The parentheses around the OR are essential.

questions.q: isAdult should be true for ages 18 and over, but it has a bug. Print age isAdult(age) for the boundary values 17, 18 and 19 to expose it, then fix the function so the output shows 17 false, 18 true, 19 true.
questions.explain: "18 and over" includes 18, so the operator is >=. Testing just below, on and just above the boundary is what reveals this kind of bug.

questions.q: A non-member shops during a sale. What does this print?
questions.explain: With parentheses, membership is required. Without them, && binds first, so the line is (false && false) || true: the sale alone gives the member discount.

questions.q: A student discount applies to ages from 16 to 25 inclusive. Write studentDiscount(age) and print the result for the boundary values 15, 16, 25 and 26, one age result pair per line.
questions.explain: "From 16 to 25 inclusive" is two comparisons joined with AND, both including their boundary. Testing one value on each side of each boundary shows both edges are right.

questions.q: Write checkTransfer(from, amount) with guards in this order: "invalid amount" unless the amount is a whole number above 0, "account frozen" when from.frozen is true, "insufficient funds" when the balance is below the amount, and "ok" otherwise.
questions.explain: "A whole number above 0" is Number.isInteger(amount) && amount > 0; its opposite, by De Morgan, is !Number.isInteger(amount) || amount <= 0. The exact balance is allowed, because the guard for funds uses <.
questions.expected:
invalid amount
account frozen
insufficient funds
ok
